# Page 3^page=3
© Idaho State University, 2020 SCOPE AND CONTENT NOTE The Fred T. Dubois papers contain his official correspondence as a United States Senator from Idaho, family correspondence, scrapbooks, newspaper clippings, speeches, subject files, ephemera, and photographs. The collection covers Dubois’ public career from his arrival in Idaho in 1880 to his death in 1930. The bulk of the collection focuses on the period from the free silver campaign of 1896 through the end of his Senate career in 1907. Researchers and scholars will find this collection useful for such subjects as free silver, anti-imperialism, forest reserves, anti-Mormonism, and Idaho politics. ARRANGEMENT When acquired, the Dubois Family Papers were separated into four collections: the Edna Dubois Papers, the Toussaint Dubois Papers, the Fred T. Dubois Papers, and the Charles E. Arney Papers, and as such, original order was compromised. The Fred T. Dubois papers are arranged into eight (8) series and eleven (11) subseries that contain materials and photographs pertaining to Dubois’ time as a two-term United States Senator representing the State of Idaho. Included in his papers are correspondence which comprises almost one-half the collection, and are arranged chronologically; subject files are organized under broad subject headings and reflect topics found in the correspondence and scrapbook files, newspaper clippings, ephemera, and photographs. Series I contains Dubois’ autobiographical material. Series II contains correspondence and is further divided into two (2) subseries: 1) general correspondence; 2) personal. Series III contains subject files that are further divided into seven (7) subseries: 1) affidavits; 2) government publications; 3) Idaho politics; 4) Mormonism; 5) travel and pensions; 6) publications; and 7) speeches. Series IV consists of scrapbooks focusing primarily on politics. Series V contains newspapers and is further divided into two (2) subseries: 1) political cartoons; and 2) newspaper clippings (dating from c. 1900-1912). Series VI consists of ephemera. Series VII contains speeches, some correspondence, broadsides, and ephemera. Series VIII contains photographs, both in albums and loose.

# Page 4^page=4
© Idaho State University, 2020 BIOGRAPHICAL NOTE Born on May 29, 1851, in Crawford County, Illinois, to Jesse and Adelia Morris Dubois, Fred was the fifth of seven children. He attended the local public schools and the Shurtleff Preparatory School in Alton, Illinois, before he and his brother Jesse K. Dubois, Jr., enrolled at Yale College in 1868. There the two brothers, who remained almost inseparable until Jesse's death in 1908, roomed together. After graduating with the Class of 1872, Jesse studied medicine while Fred returned to Illinois, where he worked for a time for the wholesale dry good house of John V. Farwell & Company in Chicago. Through family political contacts, Fred won appointment as Secretary of the Board of Railway and Warehouse Commissioners in 1875, only to resign the following year shortly before his father's death. By1880 he had decided to seek his future elsewhere. The opportunity to move to Idaho came when Jesse decided to give up his thriving medical practice and secured an appointment as physician for the Fort Hall Indian Reservation. After a brief stint as a cowboy on a cattle drive to Casper, Wyoming, Fred also found employment at Fort Hall. There he came to see possibilities for personal advancement and in 1882 used his political connections in Illinois to get an appointment as United States Marshal for Idaho Territory. Dubois married Edna Maxfield Whited, a native of Illinois, and organizer of the kindergarten movement in South Dakota. They were married in 1899 and together they had two daughters, Elizabeth Mary in 1900 and Edna Margaret (usually called Toussaint) in 1903. The family letters reveal Fred's strong affection for his wife and daughters. They also reveal how the demands of his public career and later the need to provide an adequate income through business ventures, often kept them apart as Fred remained in Washington, D.C., for most of the year while Edna looked after the Blackfoot ranch and the girls attended boarding schools. He spent most of his remaining years in Washington, D.C., where he tried to eke out a living for his family through an occasional lecture, an article on the Mormons or some other Western topic, and infrequent employment. In his later years he survived by cutting his personal living expenses, borrowing from friends and securing appointment to minor government boards. His remaining years were quieter. In 1918, as a reward for his loyalty to the Wilson administration Dubois was appointed a civilian member of the War Department's Board of Ordnance and Fortifications. Two years later he lost the post when the Republicans regained control of the White House. One last political appointment came in 1924 under the Coolidge administration. At the age of seventy-three Dubois became a Democratic member of the International Joint Commission for the Settlement of Boundary Disputes between the United States and Canada. He remained a member until his death in Washington, D.C., on February 14, 1930.

# Page 5^page=5
© Idaho State University, 2020 CHRONOLOGY 1851 Born, to Jesse and Adelia Morris Dubois, in Crawford County, Illinois, May 29 1857 Moved with his family to Springfield, Illinois 1868 Graduated from Shurtleff Preparatory School, Alton, Illinois Enrolled at Yale University 1872 Graduated from Yale University Salesman, John V. Farwell & Company in Chicago 1875-1876 Appointed Secretary of the Board of Railway and Warehouse Commissioners of the State of Illinois. He resigned the following year 1880 Moved to Idaho Territory with his brother, Dr. Jesse K. Dubois 1881 Served in various posts at the Fort Hall Indian Reservation 1882 Appointed U.S. Marshal for Idaho Territory by President Arthur Became involved in the anti-Mormon agitation over polygamy and the alleged influence of the Mormon Church in politics 1886 Elected as Territorial Delegate to Congress 1888 Elected to a second term as Territorial Delegate to Congress Became a leader in the movement to admit Idaho as a state 1890 Elected to serve as Idaho's first full-term U.S. Senator in recognition of his leadership in the statehood movement 1892 Chairman, Idaho delegation to the Republican National Convention 1893 Led the unsuccessful fight to prevent repeal of the Sherman Silver Purchase Act 1896 Walked out of the Republican National Convention and became one of the founders of the Silver Republican Party 1897 Traveled to Japan and China with his friends Frank Cannon of Utah and Richard F. Pettigrew of South Dakota 1898 Opposed U.S. annexation of the Philippine Islands following the Spanish- American War 1899 Married Edna M. Whited, a school teacher from Morrison, Illinois, January 11 1900 Elected as a Silver Republican to a second term in the U.S. Senate 1901 Announced that he was joining the Democratic Party 1902 Helped to draft the National Reclamation Act 1903 Launched a campaign to expel Reed Smoot of Utah from the U.S. Senate 1904 Attempted to place an anti-polygamy plank in both of the national party platforms 1905 Traveled to the Philippines, China and Japan with a party of congressmen and their wives; Secretary of War William Howard Taft and Alice Roosevelt led the delegation 1907 Ended his Senate career as the Republican-controlled Idaho legislature elected William E. Borah

# Page 6^page=6
© Idaho State University, 2020 1908 Published The Idaho Scimitar at Boise as a vehicle for his anti-Mormon campaign Dubois was ousted from leadership of the Idaho Democratic Party by a decision of the state supreme court in favor of the faction led by John Nugent Jessie K. Dubois, Jr. died October 31 1912 Served as floor manager of Champ Clark's bid for the Democratic presidential nomination In the fall, Dubois became regional Democratic manager for the Wilson campaign in the Pacific Northwest 1914 Failed to get the Idaho Progressive Party's nomination for U.S. Senate 1916 Served as Woodrow Wilson's Western manager 1918 Organized endorsement by the Nonpartisan League of incumbent U.S. Senators, Republican William E. Borah and Democrat John Nugent 1918-1920 Appointed by President Wilson as a civilian member of the War Department's Board of Ordnance and Fortifications 1924 Appointed by President Coolidge to the International Joint Commission for the Settlement of Boundary Disputes between the United States and Canada 1930 Died in Washington, D.C., of bronchial pneumonia and myocarditis, February 14. Buried in Blackfoot, Idaho
